record.context_brief: Unique farthest-point property in Hilbert spaces
record.original_question: Let H be a Hilbert space and let A be a closed convex subset of H with the property that every y in H has a unique farthest point in A, meaning a point of A at maximal distance from y. Must A consist of exactly one point?

evidence.quote: If a closed convex set A c H has the property that every y in H admits a unique farthest point in A (i. e. which has maximal distance from y ), does A necessarily consist of one simple point ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $H$ be a (real) Hilbert space, and let $A \subseteq H$ be a nonempty closed convex subset with the following property: for every $y \in H$, there exists a unique point $a_y \in A$ such that
$$\|y - a_y\| = \sup_{a \in A} \|y - a\|,$$
i.e., every point of $H$ admits a unique farthest point in $A$. (In particular, $A$ is bounded, since otherwise the supremum would be infinite.) Prove or disprove: $A$ must be a singleton.
artifact.status_search_result: The farthest-point (uniquely remotal set) conjecture in infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is a classical long-standing open problem, equivalent (via Klee/Ficken-type results) to the convexity of Chebyshev sets. A 2024 paper in the European Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics claims a proof that every uniquely remotal set in a Hilbert space is a singleton, but the wider acceptance of this resolution in the functional-analysis community is not clearly established in the available sources, so the status is treated as unknown.

status_evidence.snippet: Survey of partial results on whether uniquely remotal sets must be singletons.
status_evidence.claim: The problem has been a long-standing open question with only partial results.

status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of the farthest-point conjecture and partial progress.
status_evidence.claim: The farthest-point conjecture remains a central open question in the theory.
